description: Galactic Coders is a team of software Engineers united by a passion for space and technology. As part of the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to blend coding precision with the mysteries of the cosmos. With diverse skills in software, AI, and data science, we seek to create innovative solutions that inspire exploration and push boundaries proving that curiosity and code together can reach the stars.
summary: MoonMates is an interactive lunar outpost mission trainer for young explorers. Players manage Moonbase across a 15-day mission, keeping power, batteries, oxygen, water, food, crew health, radiation protection, and communications functioning. They explore a 3D outpost, complete maintenance tasks and science activities, and respond to events such as solar storms, lunar night, water leaks, and equipment failures. Their choices affect resources and system conditions, showing how protecting one part of the outpost can affect others and shape mission success. Plain-language guidance from Dr. Noor, story chapters, science discoveries, and daily reports make mission concepts engaging and accessible for ages 7–12. Players can train solo or join a crew: teammates see one another in the outpost, share task completions and event decisions, and receive crew notifications. The experience helps students explore teamwork, systems thinking, and the challenges of living on the Moon.
details:
What it does and how it works

MoonMates is a browser game where players take responsibility for a lunar outpost during a simulated 15-day mission. In first person, they explore the 3D base, travel between modules, complete maintenance and science tasks, monitor supplies and crew safety, and respond to mission events. The simulation tracks resources and system conditions over time. Task deadlines and event choices can change those values, so players see how decisions affect the outpost. Players can take on the mission alone or create/join a multiplayer crew. In crew mode, players see one another moving in the outpost and receive shared task and event updates.

Benefits and intended impact

The game turns lunar survival concepts into decisions players can make and observe, helping students understand that a Moon outpost depends on connected systems and coordinated work. It encourages systems thinking, problem solving, teamwork, and interest in space and STEM. The intended impact is to give young players an engaging way to explore what it takes to keep a lunar base operating over time, and to make those ideas accessible to classrooms, families, and curious players.

Tools, languages, and devices

The project was built with React, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Vite. Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei power the interactive 3D experience. A Node.js HTTP service supports local-network multiplayer rooms and relays supported crew updates. The game runs in a modern WebGL-capable browser on a desktop, laptop, or mobile device. Players use a keyboard and mouse or the touch movement controls; multiplayer across devices currently uses a shared local Wi-Fi/LAN connection.

Creative approach and design considerations

The project combines a walkable lunar outpost with resource management, hands-on task activities, mission events, science discoveries, Dr. Noor's guidance, and a mission story. This lets players learn through both action and explanation. During development, the team considered the target age group, clear language and controls, readable mission information, desktop and landscape mobile screens, and how to keep the mission engaging without losing sight of its educational purpose. Multiplayer was included so players can coordinate as a crew and see the effects of shared work together.

The problem and our approach

A sustained lunar presence would require crews to manage interdependent systems such as power, air, water, food, habitat safety, equipment, and communications. Routine maintenance competes with urgent incidents and science work. A solo player can experience those tradeoffs in the game; a multiplayer crew can divide attention and observe how coordinated work changes the shared mission.

The game turns that idea into a short interactive mission. Players walk through an outpost, inspect mission status and supplies, travel to equipment, complete a task activity, and make choices when an event occurs. A 15 day narrative, short science notes, and end of day reports provide context for the decisions.

Goals and learning outcomes

- Recognize that lunar base systems depend on one another and that delayed maintenance can have consequences.

- Explore tradeoffs between protecting resources, responding to incidents, and completing science work.

- Practice communicating and coordinating tasks as a crew.

- Encounter introductory facts about lunar environments, exploration, habitats, power, water ice, and Apollo missions.

- Make lunar surface exploration accessible through a browser based 3D experience.

What players can do

- Choose Single Player or Multiplayer.

- Explore a 3D lunar outpost in first person, enter supported modules, and interact with equipment.

- Use the mission HUD, live map, daily job list, resource display, science notebook, photo collection, story archive, and mission reports.

- Complete daily maintenance and resource protection challenges at designated outpost modules.

- Resolve events such as power failures, lunar night, solar storms, water leaks, fire, and water ice investigations. Choices can affect resources and system conditions.

- Work through a mission lasting up to 15 simulated lunar days, with day reports and story milestones.

- In multiplayer, create a room or join one with a six digit code, ready up, and have the host launch the crew into the lunar outpost.

- See other active crew members' avatars moving around the outpost. Receive an on screen notice when a crewmate completes a task or makes an event choice.

- Use the rover interaction and rover controls where available in the outpost.

Player journey

Single player

1. Start the experience and choose Single Player.

2. Enter the mission briefing and begin the outpost tutorial.

3. Explore the outpost and learn the controls, mission HUD, maps, jobs, and resources.

4. Follow job markers, travel to the required module, and complete the task activity.

5. Respond to mission events and review the day's report.

6. Continue through the mission story and science discoveries.

Multiplayer crew

1. Choose Multiplayer and enter a callsign.

2. Create a room and share its six digit code, or enter a code to join an existing room.

3. Each crew member marks ready. The host can start once everyone in the room is ready.

4. The clients launch into the lunar outpost using the same mission seed.

5. Players explore independently while task completion, event decisions, crew notices, and player positions are relayed to the crew.

The current room server is designed for a local network demonstration. It is not an internet hosted service.

Crew voice chat

lets players speak while exploring the outpost, dividing daily jobs, and responding to mission events together. Simple microphone and speaker icons let each player choose when to talk and whether to hear the crew. The microphone starts off and is enabled by the player.

Mission systems and content

Mission clock and resources

The simulation is configured for 15 days. A full in game day is five minutes of active play, followed by a short transition. The player monitors power, battery, oxygen, water, food, crew safety, commander safety, and science. Values are abstract percentages used by the game rules.

Jobs and events

The project includes 24 authored daily challenge definitions. Challenges are scheduled into a mission and direct players to outpost components, for example the battery container, workshop, habitat, greenhouse, solar array, rover, or communications equipment. Some critical work has urgent deadlines; missing critical tasks can mark them missed and apply configured game penalties.

Mission event definitions include six primary scenarios, with additional task consequence variants. Each event presents a situation and response choices. Outcomes can change resource levels, system conditions, and later story callbacks. The simulation also contains per task activities and tool or solution choices.

Story and science

The narrative is divided into three chapters spanning days 1–5, 6–10, and 11–15. The Science Notebook contains short lunar science discoveries unlocked during the mission. An Apollo story feature links to NASA's Apollo 11 mission overview. Science explanations and mission values are educational content and should be checked against authoritative sources before being used as factual claims beyond the game.

Controls and accessibility

The outpost starts in first person. On desktop, use W/A/S/D OR Arrow Keys to move and the mouse to look. Click the scene to capture the pointer for looking; press Esc to release it and use the cursor on interface buttons. Use Enter or E to interact with nearby prompts, and M to open the full map. Press V to return from the rover. Follow each popup's on screen key hints because individual panels can have additional controls.

On touch devices, use the on screen movement joystick and drag to look. The HUD, menus, and tutorial adapt to a landscape mobile layout. A modern browser with WebGL support is required for the 3D scene.

Technology and architecture

- Frontend: React 19, Vite 8, JavaScript and TypeScript.

- 3D: Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei; the outpost scene and player controls are implemented in the lunar outpost engine.

- Simulation: A React hook manages mission clock, seeded mission state, resources, tasks, events, and reports.

- Multiplayer: A Node.js built in HTTP server in `server/multiplayer.js`; browser clients communicate with it using JSON over HTTP.
